title: We tested 9 frontier LLMs as quant researchers. None beat the market.
author: OliviaYii
selftext:
Everyone's building AI trading agents. But can these models actually research a strategy that works on data they haven't seen?

A new benchmark called Quant-Arena puts 9 frontier LLMs through the full quant research process: build signals from real market data, backtest, iterate, and commit to one strategy.

The catch? Once committed, the strategy gets tested on a sealed 2024 dataset. No more tweaking.

**The results were pretty brutal:**

* Equal-weight market benchmark: **+17.1%**
* Best LLM strategy: **+10.7%**
* 5 out of 9 models lost money.

And here's the weird part: most models were actually better than random at ranking stocks. But the stocks they scored highest often weren't the ones generating the best returns.

One model even learned to stay in cash during a market downturn, avoiding a huge drawdown — then missed enough of the rebound to still underperform.

So maybe the bottleneck isn't generating trading ideas. It's turning decent signals into portfolios that actually make money.

Curious what people here think. Are we evaluating AI trading agents the wrong way by focusing too much on individual predictions rather than the entire research process?

replies.author: Alphanet_dogwalker
replies.body: Am i reading table 2 in the paper right that Sol at medium effort returned 18.4% against the 17.1% benchmark? Looks like the headline is about each model's highest scoring configuration, rather than every run. That's a pretty interesting distinction if the score picked a worse trading strategy than another setting of the same model.

replies.author: OliviaYii
replies.body:
Good catch! You're right, the title was a bit too broad. What we meant is that none of the nine models' highest-scoring configurations beat the market.

We don't rank models purely by annual returns. The overall score also considers risk-adjusted performance, signal quality, turnover, and results from the research period.

Sol-medium did beat the benchmark (18.4% vs. 17.1%), but had a 35.9% max drawdown and a Sharpe of 0.65. Sol-xhigh returned less (8.6%), but had a much smaller drawdown (2.8%) and a higher Sharpe (1.89).

That's why xhigh scored higher. And yes, the score and return rankings don't always line up, which is why we included all 38 configurations in the paper. Appreciate you digging into the table!

comments.author: leroylabs
comments.body: The sealed 2024 test prevents post-commit tweaking, but does it prevent pretraining contamination? For frontier models, 2024 prices and narratives may already be latent knowledge, so I’d pair Quant-Arena’s calendar holdout with synthetic or access-controlled data generated after each model’s cutoff. I’d also decompose the +10.7% best result versus the +17.1% equal-weight benchmark into rank IC, turnover, cash exposure, sector bets, and sizing. If ranking was genuinely above random, that attribution should reveal whether portfolio construction destroyed the signal or the ranking metric simply rewarded distinctions too small to trade.

replies.author: OliviaYii
replies.body:
Yeah, pretraining contamination is a real concern, and we can't completely rule it out. Frontier models may already have seen some 2024 market information during training, even if we keep that data hidden during the research process.

We've thought about two possible ways around this: using models frozen before the test period, or running forward-looking evaluations on new market data. Neither is a perfect solution though. The first makes it hard to compare current frontier models, while the second takes a long time and makes comparisons across different runs trickier.

One interesting thing is that even with potential exposure to that history, none of the highest-scoring configurations managed to beat the equal-weight benchmark. So knowing what happened in the market clearly doesn't guarantee you can turn it into a profitable strategy.

That's also part of what we're trying to measure here: given the same data access and research budget, how well can different models and workflows actually turn what they know into usable strategies?

And agreed on the attribution side. RankIC and portfolio returns tell pretty different stories in some cases. Breaking that down further by turnover, cash exposure, sector bets, etc. would be really useful.

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body: The sealed 2024 test is the right design, since the models can't tune on it. I'd be careful with one year, though, because a single period can favor one kind of strategy, and several of these gaps could shrink or flip in another year. The finding that models rank stocks better than random but still lose points at portfolio construction is the useful part. A simple check would be to take each model's signals and build the portfolio with the same fixed rules for all of them, so you can see how much comes from the signal and how much from the sizing. Cymetica's Backtest Labs is one place to test a signal with fees included.

comments.author: pulllab
comments.body: The portfolio construction point hits home. I ran a similar experiment on a smaller scale last year. The signals looked fine in isolation, but once I added position sizing and turnover costs the whole thing fell apart. Good rankings don't survive contact with real trading costs.
